next_action.label: Review shortcut-conflict attribution design
next_action.reason: Approval authorizes fork-side implementation only; no upstream action is proposed.

judgment.rationale: The report and source path establish a user-facing attribution bug, not a functional shortcut failure. The runner can only prove that temporary Win32 registration failed; it cannot prove a documented Windows-owned shortcut. The design is narrow, implementation-ready, and now has the required fork mirror trace.
evidence: The reporter reproduced on PowerToys 0.101.2362 stable / Windows 11 build 26200 after manual update.
The shortcut still opens Color Picker, so there is no functional activation failure.
A collaborator stated Win+Shift+C is historical/deprecated or generally unassigned on modern Windows 11.
The reporter suggested Windows-version gating, but that would overfit one historical chord and would not solve owner attribution for other RegisterHotKey failures.
HotkeyConflictManager::HasConflictWithSystemHotkey treats ERROR_HOTKEY_ALREADY_REGISTERED from a temporary RegisterHotKey probe as a system conflict, without owner identity.
Settings maps sysConflicts to IsSystemConflict and renders strings/link claiming a default Windows-reserved shortcut.
judgment.recommended_action: Approve the fork-side design to change system-conflict UI wording/link only, preserving the conservative detector and avoiding Windows-version whitelisting.

fix_assessment.rationale: No concrete upstream or fork implementation exists beyond the design mirror; a focused Settings UI wording/link change addresses the unsupported ownership claim while preserving conservative conflict detection.

proposed_fixes.title: Describe system hotkey conflicts as unavailable rather than Windows-owned
proposed_fixes.root_cause: The runner treats ERROR_HOTKEY_ALREADY_REGISTERED from a temporary RegisterHotKey probe as proof of a documented Windows-reserved shortcut, although the error does not identify the owner and Color Picker can still activate through the centralized keyboard hook.
plan: Revise the shared system-conflict resources in src/settings-ui/Settings.UI/Strings/en-us/Resources.resw so they describe registration failure without asserting Windows ownership.
Remove the fixed Windows shortcut documentation hyperlink from ShortcutConflictWindow.xaml while keeping the existing conflict category, Ignore action, and in-app conflict presentation.
Add Settings UI regression coverage for the revised text, absent misleading link, and unchanged Ignore behavior.
verification: Configure Color Picker to Win+Shift+C on Windows 11, open the shortcut-conflict window, confirm the warning is non-attributing and the shortcut still launches Color Picker.
Run the focused Settings UI conflict test and confirm ignored conflicts are removed from the displayed count.

confidence.rationale: The issue behavior and the runner-to-Settings resource path directly support an attribution-only fix; no detector or IPC change is required.

issue_context.summary: The conflict detector labels a functioning Color Picker chord as a Windows system conflict and points users to documentation that does not support the classification.
known_information: The configured chord is Win+Shift+C for Color Picker.
The Home screen displays one shortcut conflict.
The shortcut still opens Color Picker.
The reporter confirmed the same behavior after updating to PowerToys 0.101.2362.
A collaborator explained that Win+Shift+C is historical/deprecated or generally unassigned on modern Windows 11.
The reporter then suggested the warning may be too indiscriminate and Windows-version-specific.
No assignee, duplicate, or linked fix is present.
inferences: A failed temporary RegisterHotKey probe can establish that Windows did not grant that registration in that environment, but it cannot establish that a documented default Windows shortcut owns the chord.

Because Color Picker uses the centralized keyboard hook, successful activation does not prove the registration probe is wrong; it proves the current unassignable/default-system wording overstates the observed behavior.
Windows-version gating for Win+Shift+C would be an overfit because hotkey availability can vary by build, installed apps, policy, and session.
issue_context.analysis: The runner maps a failed temporary Win32 registration directly to SystemConflict, serializes it as sysConflicts, and the Settings UI renders that category as a default system shortcut reserved by Windows with a link to the public shortcut list. RegisterHotKey exposes no owner identity, and the report demonstrates a chord that still activates Color Picker but is not documented by the linked page. Preserve the warning as a conservative unavailable-to-register result, but make its text explicitly non-attributing and remove the evidence-implying link. This requires no IPC schema or detector behavior change.
initial_investigation: Reviewed the complete issue body, all four comments including the 2026-09-03 version-gating suggestion, labels, assignees, project items, timeline, and duplicate search results.
src/runner/powertoy_module.cpp::PowertoyModule::update_hotkeys calls HotkeyConflictManager::AddHotkey, then registers module activation with CentralizedKeyboardHook::SetHotkeyAction.
src/runner/hotkey_conflict_detector.cpp::HasConflictWithSystemHotkey performs the temporary RegisterHotKey probe; GetHotkeyConflictsAsJson serializes positive results as sysConflicts.
src/settings-ui/Settings.UI/Strings/en-us/Resources.resw and ShortcutConflictWindow.xaml currently say System shortcut/reserved by Windows and show the fixed Windows shortcut documentation link.
Created fork mirror issue 582 after confirming no existing [Issue 50239] mirror issue was present.

design.root_cause: The UI attribution is stronger than the evidence produced by the runner. HotkeyConflictManager::HasConflictWithSystemHotkey only observes that a temporary RegisterHotKey(nullptr, 0x0FFF, modifiers, key) call failed with ERROR_HOTKEY_ALREADY_REGISTERED. That error does not identify the owner and cannot distinguish documented Windows reservations from another process, shell state, policy, or environment-specific registration. AddHotkey stores the result as SystemConflict, Settings preserves it as IsSystemConflict, and resources/XAML present it as a documented, unassignable Windows shortcut. Color Picker remains able to activate through CentralizedKeyboardHook, so the unconditional reserved/default-system explanation is false for this report.
evidence: Issue 50239 reproduces on PowerToys 0.101.2362 / Windows 11 build 26200: Home reports a system conflict for Win+Shift+C, the linked Windows shortcut page has no entry, and Color Picker still opens.
A collaborator describes Win+Shift+C as historical/deprecated or generally unassigned on modern Windows 11.
src/runner/powertoy_module.cpp::PowertoyModule::update_hotkeys both calls HotkeyConflictManager::AddHotkey and installs the module action through CentralizedKeyboardHook::SetHotkeyAction.

src/runner/hotkey_conflict_detector.cpp::HasConflictWithSystemHotkey returns true solely for ERROR_HOTKEY_ALREADY_REGISTERED after a temporary RegisterHotKey attempt, and GetHotkeyConflictsAsJson emits sysConflicts.
src/settings-ui/Settings.UI/Strings/en-us/Resources.resw and ShortcutConflictWindow.xaml use that category to display System shortcut, reserved-by-Windows wording, and a Windows-shortcuts hyperlink.

affected_files.purpose: Defines the English tooltip, card heading, and description displayed for every conflict currently classified as a system conflict.
Renders the detailed shortcut-conflict card and contains the fixed Windows shortcut documentation URI.
New Settings UI regression coverage for the system-conflict card wording and absence of an unsupported Windows-shortcuts destination.

implementation_steps.current_behavior: All sysConflicts use text that says the shortcut is already used by a default system shortcut, label the card 'System shortcut', say it is reserved by Windows and cannot be reassigned, and offer 'See all Windows shortcuts'.
implementation_steps.change: Keep the existing resource keys and the IsSystemConflict transport category, but revise the English strings to describe an unavailable shortcut without asserting ownership or permanent reservation. For example: tooltip 'PowerToys could not register this shortcut. It may be used or reserved by Windows or another app.'; header 'Shortcut unavailable'; description 'PowerToys could not register this shortcut. Choose another shortcut or ignore this warning if it works as expected.' Remove the link-content resource when step 2 removes its only consumer. Route changed English resources through the normal localization process rather than hand-editing translated files.
implementation_steps.code_block:
<data name="SysHotkeyConflictTooltipText" xml:space="preserve">
  <value>PowerToys could not register this shortcut. It may be used or reserved by Windows or another app.</value>
</data>
<data name="ShortcutConflictWindow_SystemCard.Header" xml:space="preserve">
  <value>Shortcut unavailable</value>
</data>
<data name="ShortcutConflictWindow_SystemCard.Description" xml:space="preserve">
  <value>PowerToys could not register this shortcut. Choose another shortcut or ignore this warning if it works as expected.</value>
</data>
edge_cases: Do not describe an ERROR_HOTKEY_ALREADY_REGISTERED result as proof that either Windows or another app owns the shortcut.
Keep in-app conflict text unchanged because hotkeyMap and inAppConflictHotkeyMap identify a PowerToys module.
Do not remove the existing Ignore shortcut affordance; it is the safe escape hatch for a warning whose source cannot be attributed.
Avoid changing resource keys unless every compiled reference and localization entry is migrated together.
tests: Build Settings.UI and verify all existing SysHotkeyConflictTooltipText consumers compile without resource lookup regressions.
In the new UI test, supply a SystemConflicts group and assert the visible tooltip/card uses the revised non-attributing strings.

implementation_steps.current_behavior: When HotkeyConflictGroupData.ShouldShowSysConflict is true, the conflict window shows a Windows-logo card and always renders a HyperlinkButton to a generic Microsoft Windows shortcut list, implying that list identifies the detected owner.
implementation_steps.change: Retain the SystemConflictCard visibility binding, module cards, and Ignore behavior, but remove the fixed HyperlinkButton and its Windows-specific comment. The revised card remains an availability explanation, not a source-attribution panel. No runner-to-Settings JSON contract changes: sysConflicts and IsSystemConflict continue to drive the same layout path.
implementation_steps.code_block:
<tkcontrols:SettingsCard
    x:Name="SystemConflictCard"
    x:Uid="ShortcutConflictWindow_SystemCard"
    ...
    IsEnabled="{x:Bind ShouldShowSysConflict, Mode=OneTime}">
    <tkcontrols:SettingsCard.HeaderIcon>...</tkcontrols:SettingsCard.HeaderIcon>
</tkcontrols:SettingsCard>
<!-- Remove ShortcutConflictWindow_SystemShortcutLink and its fixed NavigateUri. -->
edge_cases: Leave the card hidden for ignored conflicts through ShouldShowSysConflict.
Do not change card navigation, the conflict count, or the enabled shortcut editor.
Confirm keyboard and screen-reader focus no longer reaches a dead or misleading hyperlink.
tests: Extend ShortcutConflictTests.SystemConflict_UsesNonAttributingAvailabilityText to assert no control with the removed link automation identifier/URI is present.

Manually open the shortcut-conflicts window with a real system-classified chord, verify the revised card is accessible in light, dark, and high-contrast themes, and verify Ignore still removes it from the count.

implementation_steps.current_behavior: Runner unit coverage only verifies an in-app duplicate in HotkeyConflictTests::HasConflict_TwoModulesSameHotkey_InAppConflict; there is no end-to-end regression that guards the user-facing wording for a sysConflicts payload.
implementation_steps.change: Add a focused Settings UI test using the existing Settings test host/IPC seam to deliver an all_hotkey_conflicts response containing one sysConflicts group for ColorPicker's activation shortcut. Open the dashboard conflict window, assert the revised availability header/description and tooltip, assert that the old reservation wording and Windows shortcut link are absent, then exercise Ignore and assert the conflict count falls to zero.
edge_cases: Make the test assert resource-derived visible text or automation properties rather than a Windows-logo icon.
Reset the ignored-hotkey test state in setup/teardown so other Settings UI tests remain order-independent.
Do not use a live RegisterHotKey result in automated tests; it varies by Windows build, installed applications, session, and elevation.
tests: Run the existing Settings UI shortcut/conflict test subset in the same test assembly.

verify: Build the affected Settings UI project: from src\settings-ui, run tools\build\build.cmd (or the repository-supported equivalent that builds Settings.UI).
Build and run the Settings UI UI-test project containing ShortcutConflictTests with vstest.console.exe and a fully-qualified-name filter for SystemConflict_UsesNonAttributingAvailabilityText.
Run src\runner\UnitTests\UnitTests-Runner.vcxproj through the existing Runner unit-test binary to confirm the unchanged in-app conflict behavior still passes.

Manual E2E on Windows 11: set Color Picker to Win+Shift+C, open Home then the shortcut-conflicts window, confirm the warning no longer calls it a default/reserved Windows shortcut and no Windows-shortcuts link is shown; confirm Color Picker still launches and Ignore removes the dashboard count.
Manual negative case: configure a known duplicate PowerToys shortcut and confirm it still uses the distinct 'another utility' wording and remains listed as an in-app conflict.
risks: The conservative warning remains even when the centralized keyboard hook can activate the chord, so some users may still see a warning; the design intentionally fixes the unsupported attribution rather than claiming the detector can reliably prove usability.
Changing a shared system-conflict resource affects every module, not only Color Picker. That is required because every consumer currently receives the same unproven ownership claim.
Removing the generic link reduces a troubleshooting path for genuinely Windows-reserved shortcuts, but leaving it falsely presents a non-authoritative list as proof of ownership.
New English resource text requires normal localization handling; incomplete localization could cause fallback English or inconsistent wording until translations land.
Changing sysConflicts semantics or the IPC model instead would affect runner lifetime and Settings UI parsing; this design deliberately avoids that broader compatibility risk.
alternatives: Whitelist Win+Shift+C on Windows 11: rejected because reservation behavior can vary by Windows version, policy, shell features, installed software, and session.
Treat every RegisterHotKey failure as no conflict when a centralized hook exists: rejected because it would hide useful warnings for genuinely unavailable chords.
Add a third unknown external conflict IPC category: rejected for this issue because the detector still cannot identify the owner and the wording-only fix avoids compatibility churn.
Keep the system shortcut label but soften only the description: rejected because both the header and Microsoft documentation link assert unsupported system ownership.
Show the raw Win32 error: rejected because ERROR_HOTKEY_ALREADY_REGISTERED is not actionable for end users and does not identify the owner.

title: Shortcut Conflict shown when there's no documented conflict.
author: gungfujoe
summary: PowerToys reports Win+Shift+C as a Windows system shortcut conflict even though Color Picker still activates; the implementation-grade design fixes unsupported Windows-reservation wording and removes the misleading documentation link while preserving conservative conflict detection.

mirror.fork_title: [Issue 50239] Shortcut Conflict shown when there is no documented conflict.

non_blocking_notes: Keep the change scoped to attribution wording/link removal.
Do not version-gate a single historical shortcut.
